title: Crispy Corn: How to Make the Restaurant-Style Spicy Snack at Home
excerpt: Golden, spice-dusted sweet corn kernels with a shattering crunch — here is how to nail the Indian restaurant starter at home, plus the details that keep it crisp.
body:
• Crispy corn is a popular Indian restaurant-style starter: boiled sweet corn kernels coated in cornflour and rice flour, deep-fried until crisp.
  • The keys to crunch are draining the kernels thoroughly, keeping the coating thin and dry, and frying at 175 to 180°C (347 to 356°F).
  • The hot kernels are tossed in a dry seasoning of chaat masala, red chilli powder, roasted cumin, black pepper and black salt, finished with coriander and lemon.
  • Serve immediately — the coating softens as it cools, so this is a make-and-eat snack, not a make-ahead one.

What Crispy Corn Is

Crispy corn is the kind of bar snack Indian restaurants have turned into a quiet obsession: sweet corn kernels with a shattering, golden coating, tossed in a spicy-tangy masala and eaten too fast to talk. The coating is crisp while the corn inside stays tender and mildly sweet, and it arrives at the table hot enough that the seasoning clings to every kernel.

Recreating it at home is straightforward, though it rewards attention to detail. The method below is adapted from the widely followed recipe by Dassana Amit of Veg Recipes of India: kernels are boiled briefly, coated in two rounds of flour, deep-fried in small batches, and seasoned while still hot. Frozen sweet corn works if you have no fresh cobs — just thaw it, cook it for only a couple of minutes and drain it very well.

The Recipe

Ingredients

  • 2 cups sweet corn kernels (from about 2 medium corn cobs)
  • 4 cups water and ½ teaspoon salt, for boiling
  • 4 tablespoons cornflour (white cornstarch, not corn flour or cornmeal)
  • 2 tablespoons rice flour (or all-purpose flour)
  • ½ teaspoon salt and ¼ teaspoon black pepper powder, for the coating
  • ½ teaspoon red chilli powder, 1 teaspoon chaat masala, ¼ teaspoon roasted cumin powder, ¼ teaspoon black pepper powder, ¼ teaspoon black salt — the seasoning mix
  • 2 cups oil (or as needed) for deep-frying
  • 1 tablespoon chopped coriander leaves and 1–2 teaspoons lemon juice, to finish

Method

  1. Slice the kernels from the cobs, keeping the knife close to the cob so the kernels stay whole. Discard any that are cut open or crushed — their exposed moisture will splatter in hot oil.
  2. Bring the water and salt to a boil, add the kernels, and boil for 4 to 5 minutes. Do not overcook; soft kernels are hard to coat and fry.
  3. Drain the kernels very well and spread them on a plate to cool and dry. They should be only lightly moist, with no water dripping, so the flour sticks evenly.
  4. Mix the red chilli powder, chaat masala, roasted cumin, black pepper and black salt in a small bowl. Keep the seasoning ready before you start frying.
  5. Transfer the cooled kernels to a wide bowl. Add half the cornflour and rice flour with the salt and black pepper, and toss until each kernel is coated. Add the remaining flour and toss again. If the coating will not stick, sprinkle in water a teaspoon at a time (no more than 3 teaspoons); if it turns pasty, add a little more cornflour.
  6. Tip the coated kernels into a sieve and shake gently to remove loose flour, which would otherwise burn in the oil.
  7. Heat the oil in a deep, heavy kadai or pan to 175 to 180°C (347 to 356°F). A test kernel should rise quickly and fry with steady bubbles without browning at once.
  8. Add the coated corn in small batches. Stir once gently with a long-handled slotted spoon to separate the kernels, then cover with a splatter screen or a partially open lid — kernels can pop. After about a minute, remove the cover and fry for 3 to 4 minutes total, until crisp and light golden and the sizzling has eased.
  9. Lift the corn out with a slotted spoon and drain briefly in a single layer on kitchen paper. Let the oil return to temperature before frying the next batch.
  10. While still hot, transfer the corn to a bowl, sprinkle the seasoning over it and toss immediately. Mix in the coriander leaves and 1 teaspoon lemon juice, taste, and add the second teaspoon of lemon juice or a pinch of salt only if needed.
  11. Serve at once. Do not let it cool — the coating turns chewy as it sits.

Tips for Maximum Crisp

The coating should be thin and dry, not thick or pasty; excess moisture is the enemy at every stage. Fry in small batches so the oil temperature holds, and never cover the kadai tightly, since trapped steam condenses and drips into the oil. Season the corn the moment it leaves the paper — the dry spices adhere far better to hot, crisp kernels — and go easy on the lemon juice, which can soften the coating if overdone.

Leftovers will not keep their crunch, though a few minutes in an air fryer or hot oven can revive them slightly. Better to fry only what you will eat: boil extra corn, refrigerate it well-drained for up to a day, and coat and fry fresh for the next round.
